name: Istiqlal Mosque
label: Istiqlal Mosque
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Katedral Jakarta' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Katedral Jakarta' (way/97196698): middle (85 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/9627236: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Masjid Istiqlal' (344 m across).
notes: Southeast Asia's largest mosque, with a modernist design.

text.description: Istiqlal Mosque is the national mosque of Indonesia and the largest in Southeast Asia. It opened to the public on 22 February 1978. Its name means 'Independence', and the number 45 is built into it: the central dome is 45 metres across, for 1945, the year of independence. It stands beside Merdeka Square, with Jakarta Cathedral and Immanuel Church close by, a position President Sukarno chose to symbolise religious harmony. That is why the best phone photo here includes more than the mosque. From the cathedral's front plaza, across the road, you can fit the white dome and facade of the mosque and the cathedral's spires into one frame. The marble and the stainless steel patterns were cleaned in a major renovation finished in 2020, so the building looks crisp in clear light. Start with a wide shot to show both buildings and the road between them. Then zoom in on the dome and facade for a tighter picture. Watch the edges of the frame for traffic and street furniture, and tilt the phone slightly rather than leaning back. If you are allowed into the grounds, the courtyard with its pillars and the tall minaret seen from below make good second pictures.
text.geographic_location: Istiqlal Mosque is in Jakarta, next to Merdeka Square. It sits directly across the road from Jakarta Cathedral, and Immanuel Church is also close by.
text.directions_text: Head for Merdeka Square and Jakarta Cathedral (Katedral Jakarta). From there the mosque is to the south-west, about 4 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the mosque, the road and the cathedral. Switch to 2x or 3x telephoto if your phone has it, to pick out the dome and facade. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want to include the cathedral spires from close up, and check the edges for stretched shapes.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Katedral Jakarta (front plaza, on the side of the road facing the mosque). The mosque's dome and facade framed across the road, with the cathedral's spires often included in the same frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the vertical lines straight, so the buildings do not lean. Put the dome near the upper third and let the cathedral spires fill one side to show the two buildings together. For a different view, go into the mosque grounds if allowed: the white mosque across the open pillared courtyard, or the minaret shot from below for a dramatic upward angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white marble to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the facade keeps its detail and does not turn pure white. Take a few frames, as passing vehicles will spoil some of them.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Clear mornings or the softer light later in the afternoon usually suit white marble better than harsh midday sun. Early in the day there is also usually less traffic and fewer people on the plaza.

text.access_note: The mosque is a working place of worship; photography during Friday prayers and major celebrations is restricted and visitor access inside may be limited, so check the official site before you go.

name: Ancol Dreamland
label: Ancol Dreamland
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/28845528: large area 'Ancol Dreamland Theme Park' (4181 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: A large seafront recreation park on Jakarta Bay.

text.description: Ancol Dreamland, or Taman Impian Jaya Ancol, is a huge waterfront leisure area on Jakarta's northern shore, and it works well as a spot for varied phone photos. It opened in 1966 on land that was once swamp and fish ponds, and it is described as the largest integrated tourism area in Southeast Asia. It covers about 552 hectares, with beaches, hotels, a marina, an oceanarium, an art market and the Dunia Fantasi theme park (Dufan), which opened on 29 August 1985 and faces the Java Sea. For photos, the appeal is the mix: bright rides, the Bianglala ferris wheel, themed buildings and the open sea in one place. Because the area is so large, the subject is a whole area rather than a single building, so treat it as a starting point and wander. Look for colourful ride structures against the sky, people enjoying the beach, and boats near the marina. Keep your phone lens clean, as sea air and sunscreen smudge it quickly. Try a few frames of the same scene at different zoom levels, and keep moving rides sharp by holding the phone steady against your body. Attractions such as Dunia Fantasi are ticketed, so check the official site for entry rules before you go.
text.geographic_location: Ancol Dreamland lies in the Ancol area of Pademangan, North Jakarta, along the city's waterfront beside the Bay of Jakarta and the Java Sea. It is part of the Ancol Bay City resort.
text.directions_text: No station is listed close to this spot, so travel to Ancol or Pademangan in North Jakarta by whatever local transport suits you. The phone icon on the map is about 530 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for general scenes of rides and walkways. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for big structures or the open shoreline, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out ride details, signs or a ferris wheel from a distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 530 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place a ride, the ferris wheel or a building on one of the thirds, leaving sky or sea in the rest of the frame. Use ultra-wide from low down to make tall structures look bigger, and the telephoto lens for close, uncluttered details. Try a Live Photo of moving rides, then pick the best frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky to lock focus, then slide the exposure down a little so colours stay rich and the sky does not wash out. Use portrait mode for friends in front of a colourful backdrop.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon usually brings softer light and cooler weather, and the park lights can look good at dusk; use night mode if you stay on after dark.

text.access_note: Ancol Dreamland is a large resort area with ticketed attractions such as Dunia Fantasi, so check the official site before you go for entry rules.

name: National Monument (Monas)
label: Monas
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Medan Merdeka' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Jalan Medan Merdeka Utara' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1159084257: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'National Monument' (132 m across).
notes: The 132 m obelisk topped with a gilded flame, standing in Merdeka Square.

text.description:
Monas is the tall, slim tower that anchors Merdeka Square in Central Jakarta. It rises 132 metres and is topped with a flame covered in gold leaf, built to commemorate the struggle for Indonesian independence. Building began in 1961 under President Sukarno and it opened to the public in 1975. The architect worked the numbers 17, 8 and 45 into its dimensions, for the proclamation date of 17 August 1945. The obelisk is clad in pale Italian marble, so it stands out clearly against the sky.

The tower photographs best from a distance, where the whole shape fits in one frame. The open plaza around it gives you room to step back, and the city skyline sits behind it. Medan Merdeka is the classic wide-angle position and is free to walk around. For the best shot, stand in the north-eastern part of the plaza, on the Istiqlal side. Keep the tower in the middle of the frame and leave some sky above the flame. If you have time, try a second angle from Taman Lapangan Banteng, a park beside the square, where trees and lawn frame the monument. Another option is a close, upward view from the ground at the base. The viewing deck at the top is small and crowded, and it may charge extra for cameras, so check the official site before you go. The dancing fountain runs on weekend evenings and can make a good subject.
text.geographic_location: Monas stands in the centre of Merdeka Square (Medan Merdeka) in Central Jakarta, in front of the Presidential Palace.
text.directions_text: Head for Merdeka Square in Central Jakarta and walk to the north-eastern side of the plaza, on the Istiqlal side. Parts of the park may be fenced off because of building work, so you may need to walk around them. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the tower, the plaza and the sky in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner view of the tower with the city behind it. Use the telephoto (2x-5x) to pick out the golden flame at the top without walking closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Medan Merdeka (open plaza around the monument, best from the northeast part near the Istiqlal side). A wide view of the monument rising from the middle of the open plaza, with the city behind it. The monument is to the south-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the tower on a vertical line so it stands straight. Hold the phone level, because tilting it upwards makes the tower lean. Leave some open plaza in the foreground to give a sense of scale. For a second angle, try Taman Lapangan Banteng, where trees and lawn frame the monument.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the white marble does not wash out. In the ultra-wide, keep the tower away from the edges of the frame, where it can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise or the golden hour before sunset, when the sky has the best colours.

text.access_note: The plaza around the monument is open public space that is free to walk around, but the tower, museum and viewing deck may be ticketed or have restricted times, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Tilting the phone upwards makes tall buildings appear to lean in the frame.
The pale marble tower stands out clearly against the sky.
The ultra-wide lens can stretch objects near the edges of the frame.

name: National Museum of Indonesia
label: National Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Museum Nasional' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Museum Nasional' (node/4324721689): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/9123397: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'National Museum of Indonesia' (204 m across).
notes: The 'Elephant Museum', named for the bronze elephant out front.

text.description: The National Museum of Indonesia is better known as the Elephant Museum, and the reason is standing right in its front garden: a bronze elephant, given to Batavia by King Chulalongkorn of Siam in 1871. The museum opened in 1868, and the older wing, Gedung Gajah, is the one with the pale colonial facade and rows of columns. It is the side most people want in their photos. Inside, the collections run from prehistoric finds to classical Hindu-Buddhist statues, with about 141,000 objects in total. From there you take in the whole frontage, and the bronze elephant should be in front of you if it is visible from that spot. The forecourt by the elephant is a separate spot a little further in. There the bronze elephant sits in the foreground with the white columns behind it. The elephant adds scale and gives the building a clear subject, so the shot works even on a busy day. Take one wide shot of the whole frontage, then a closer one of the elephant with the columns softly behind it. If you have time, walk out to Jalan Medan Merdeka Barat for a second view of the frontage from the street, with the greenery of Merdeka Square alongside. The museum was closed for renovation after a fire in September 2023 and reopened in October 2024. Some work in the old wing may still be going on, so the forecourt may look different from older photos.
text.geographic_location: The museum is on Jalan Medan Merdeka Barat in Central Jakarta, on the west side of Merdeka Square.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Merdeka Square in Central Jakarta and head for its west side, where the museum fronts Jalan Medan Merdeka Barat. Ask for Museum Nasional, also called Museum Gajah. For the closer elephant shot, walk into the front forecourt. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the facade, and for the elephant too if it is in view. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want every column in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (front forecourt, standing near the bronze elephant statue and facing the colonial facade of the Gedung Gajah wing). The white colonial facade with its columns, with the bronze elephant in the foreground. For a closer view, walk into the front forecourt by the elephant.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Where the elephant is in view, put it low in the frame, off-centre, and let the columns rise behind it. Turn on gridlines and keep the verticals straight so the building doesn't lean. For a second picture, try the street-side view from Jalan Medan Merdeka Barat, which shows the whole frontage with the Merdeka Square trees beside it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright and the building looks washed out. Try portrait mode on the elephant if the background is cluttered, but check the edges around the tusks and ears.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Earlier or later in the day usually gives softer light on the facade and fewer people in the forecourt. Midday sun can be harsh on white walls.

text.access_note: The museum may be ticketed, and parts of the old wing may be affected by renovation, so check the official site before you go.

name: Selamat Datang Monument
label: Selamat Datang
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Halte Bundaran HI Astra' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Halte Bundaran HI ASTRA' (way/1226072557): middle (158 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/318076752: the OpenStreetMap point 'Welcome Monument'.
notes: The Welcome Monument statue in the middle of the Hotel Indonesia roundabout.

text.description:
Two bronze figures, a man and a woman, stand with arms raised in welcome above a ring of fountains in the middle of one of Jakarta's busiest roundabouts. The woman holds a bouquet of flowers. The Selamat Datang (Welcome) Monument was finished in 1962 by the sculptor Edhi Sunarso, from a design sketched by Henk Ngantung. It was built ahead of the Asian Games IV to show the country's openness to visitors. Each figure is about five metres tall, and with its pedestal the whole monument reaches roughly thirty metres above the ground.

It photographs well because the statues are bold and simple, with the fountain pool around them and glass towers behind. The monument sits in the traffic itself and cannot be approached, so the best pictures are taken from a raised position. From there you look down on the figures and the fountain ring with the roundabout and the towers beyond, and the roads are not the main subject.

A second raised option is the Infinity Bridge at Bundaran HI, which gives a clear view of the monument with the skyline around it. On Sunday mornings the roundabout fills with joggers, cyclists and street photographers during Car-Free Day. That makes lively pictures but also a busier deck.
text.geographic_location: In Central Jakarta, at the centre of the Bundaran Hotel Indonesia (Bundaran HI) roundabout on Jalan M.H. Thamrin, next to Hotel Indonesia. Jalan Imam Bonjol, Jalan Sutan Syahrir and Jalan Kebon Kacang also meet here.
text.directions_text: Head for the Bundaran HI roundabout on Jalan M.H. Thamrin in Central Jakarta and go to the Bundaran HI Astra Transjakarta shelter. From there the monument is about 165 m to the south, though it sits inside the traffic circle, so enjoy it from where you are. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the statues, the fountain ring and the roundabout together. Switch to telephoto (2x or 3x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the two figures and their raised arms. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the surrounding towers and the whole circle in view.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Halte Bundaran HI Astra (second-floor observation deck on the south side of the Transjakarta shelter). A raised, close view down onto the bronze statues and fountain ring, with the roundabout and surrounding towers behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place the figures on one of the vertical lines, with the towers filling the space behind. Keep the horizon level, because the tall buildings show any tilt. For a different angle, try the Infinity Bridge at Bundaran HI, which gives a clear view of the monument with the skyline around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the statues to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the bronze keeps its detail. In the evening, use night mode and rest your elbows on the railing to keep the phone still. Wipe the lens first.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light. After dark the fountains and lighting make a good night-mode shot. Sunday mornings during Car-Free Day are lively but crowded, with queues for the deck.

text.access_note: The monument stands in an active traffic roundabout and cannot be approached, so view it from the pavements, the bridge or the shelter deck. The deck is a public viewing platform, but you may need a Transjakarta or similar travel card to get through security, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning and late afternoon usually give softer light for photographs.
The fountains and lighting at the roundabout look good after dark.
Weekday mornings and afternoons are likely to be quieter on the deck than Sunday Car-Free Day.
Resting your elbows on the deck railing can help keep a phone steady in night mode.

name: Gambir railway station
label: Gambir Station
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Medan Merdeka' (4 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Jalan Medan Merdeka Timur' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/4891132084: the OpenStreetMap point 'Gambir'.
notes: The main intercity railway station, next to Merdeka Square.

text.description: Gambir is a major railway station and the terminus for most intercity trains across Java, and it is a surprisingly photogenic building. It stands on the eastern side of Merdeka Square, next to Immanuel Church. The present building opened in June 1992 and replaced an older Art Deco station. It is a modern design that borrows from the traditional joglo style, with a lime green ceramic facade and moss green platform poles. The green was chosen to sit well beside the park on the square. The station's columns were also placed so that the National Monument can be seen from Jalan Medan Merdeka Timur. That makes the monument and the station natural partners in one picture. The station site goes back much further, with a station called Weltevreden opening here in 1884. What makes a good photo is the colour and the strong horizontal roofline. For a different view, the grounds around Monas on Medan Merdeka let you look south-east across the open square towards the station. If you want a closer, street-level look at the facade, Jalan Medan Merdeka Timur is another alternative. Keep your photos to the outside of the building. Gambir is a working station, so expect people and vehicles to pass through your frame.
text.geographic_location: Gambir station is in the Gambir district of Central Jakarta, on the eastern edge of Merdeka Square (Medan Merdeka). It stands next to Immanuel Church and the Pramuka Movement headquarters.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. The station is on the eastern side of Merdeka Square, the well-known area around the Monas monument. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to capture the station and some of its surroundings. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the facade does not fit, and use the telephoto (2x or more) to pick out the roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Medan Merdeka (grounds around Monas, looking southeast toward the station). The station's exterior and roofline framed in the open square, with the Monas monument in the foreground. Turn towards the station, which lies to the north-west, and frame the facade and roofline from there.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the roofline along one of the horizontal lines. Try the telephoto to compress the scene and focus on the green facade. For a different view, try Jalan Medan Merdeka Timur, which shows the facade at street level with the square behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the green keeps its colour. Hold the phone level to keep the vertical lines straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, before sunset, when the golden-hour light falls on the green facade.

text.access_note: The Monas grounds are free to enter and the station is a working transport building, so check the official site before you go if you plan to go inside.

name: Jakarta History Museum
label: Fatahillah Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Taman Fatahillah' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Taman Fatahillah' (way/368542626): middle (177 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/4243812179: the OpenStreetMap point 'Jakarta History Museum'.
notes: The former Batavia city hall, on the south side of Fatahillah Square.

text.description: The Jakarta History Museum fills the south side of Taman Fatahillah, the old Batavia city square in Kota Tua. The building was finished in 1710 as the Stadhuis, the city hall of Dutch-ruled Batavia, and it became a museum in 1974. It is modelled on the Paleis op de Dam in Amsterdam, which explains the domed cupola and the formal, symmetrical front. It photographs well because the square in front is wide and open, so the whole facade fits in one frame with space around it. A fountain in the middle of the square gives you something for the foreground. Inside, the museum has about 23,500 objects and 37 rooms, but photography indoors is restricted and flash is not allowed, so the square is where you will take your best pictures. The square is a public open space. Weekends are busy, so a weekday or early-morning visit gives you a cleaner view. If you want a second angle, Cafe Batavia on the square has an upper floor that looks across to the museum, though you would need to go in as a customer.
text.geographic_location: In the Old Town (Kota Tua) of Jakarta, on the south side of Fatahillah Square. It stands close to the Wayang Museum and the Fine Art and Ceramic Museum.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so simply head for Kota Tua and Fatahillah Square. Once you are on the square, the museum fills the south side. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole facade, the fountain and plenty of open square in one shot. The default lens (1x) gives a calmer, more natural view of the building. If people are in the way, use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the cupola and the central part of the front.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Taman Fatahillah (from the open square, facing the museum's front facade). The museum's colonial facade framed by the open square, ideally with the central fountain in the foreground. From here the building sits in a clear, uncluttered frame, and the central fountain can be kept in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the building up with the centre of the frame so the symmetry looks deliberate. Keep the phone level so the walls do not lean. Crouch slightly to bring the fountain into the bottom of the picture. Cafe Batavia's upper floor is an alternative if you want a higher view across the square with the museum behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright so the walls keep their colour and detail. A Live Photo can be useful here, because you can pick the frame where nobody is crossing in front of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when guides say the light is softer and the square is less crowded.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but the museum is a visitor site with restricted indoor photography, so check opening days and hours before you go.

name: Jakarta Cathedral
label: Jakarta Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lapangan Banteng' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Lapangan Banteng' (way/28705164): middle (591 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/97196698: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Jakarta Cathedral' (85 m across).
notes: Neo-Gothic cathedral right across the street from Istiqlal Mosque.

text.description:
Jakarta Cathedral, officially the Church of Our Lady of the Assumption, is the seat of the Archbishop of Jakarta. Its plastered walls over thick red brick and its tall pointed spires stand out among the buildings of Central Jakarta. The present church was built between 1891 and 1901, after the earlier building collapsed in 1890, and was designed in the neo-Gothic style. The architect Marius Hulswit simplified the original plan and used cast-iron spires. The two tallest spires are 60 metres high and flank the main doorway. A third, shorter spire of 45 metres rises over the middle of the church. The south tower still has working old clocks.

The cathedral photographs well because of the strong vertical lines of the twin towers against open sky. Its neighbour, the Istiqlal Mosque, gives the area a distinctive character. The full front is hard to fit in from close range, so use the open lawns of Lapangan Banteng, where you can step back and take in the whole building. Walk around the grass to find a clear gap between trees and lamp posts. Keep the phone level so the towers do not lean. Take a few frames from different spots, because the building looks quite different from each side. Exterior photos from public areas are generally fine, but photography is not allowed during Mass and flash should be avoided. Please keep a respectful distance from worshippers.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral is in Central Jakarta, near Merdeka Square and Merdeka Palace, at the northern corner of the Lapangan Banteng park. The Istiqlal Mosque stands next to it.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, rail or tram stops listed for this spot, so head for the Lapangan Banteng area of Central Jakarta. The cathedral address is Jl. Katedral No. 7B. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit both spires and the whole front into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view of the building. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the spire tops, the clock and the rose window.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Lapangan Banteng (Park grounds beside the cathedral's position at the park's northern corner; walk around the open lawn to find the frame). The neo-Gothic facade and twin spires seen across open park space, with the Istiqlal Mosque and monument nearby in the wider frame. The main front faces west, so for a straight-on view of it, walk round towards the Istiqlal side.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the towers with the vertical lines so they stand straight. Keep a strip of lawn or sky in the picture to show the building's size. For a different view, you can also cross the street to the Masjid Istiqlal grounds and frame the cathedral's front and spires from the opposite side, with the mosque's grounds in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the plastered walls to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky does not wash out the spires. Keep the flash off. Try panorama only if you hold the phone very steady, as buildings can bend at the edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon is likely to suit the west-facing main front, which you can reach by walking round towards the Istiqlal side, but choose a time outside Mass, when photography is not allowed.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the public park and street, but for going inside, the museum or Mass times, check the official site before you go, and dress respectfully as it is a place of worship.
claims_not_in_sources: Late afternoon sun is likely to light the west-facing front of the cathedral.
Panorama mode can bend vertical lines of buildings near the edges of the frame.
Trees and lamp posts in the park may block parts of the view, so walking around the lawn helps to find a clear gap.

name: Fatahillah Square
label: Fatahillah Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Museum Sejarah Jakarta' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Museum Sejarah Jakarta' (node/4243812179): point; moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/368542626: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Taman Fatahillah' (178 m across).
notes: The main square of Jakarta's old Dutch colonial town, Batavia.

text.description: Fatahillah Square (Taman Fatahillah) is the old heart of Batavia, the Dutch-era city that became Jakarta. Today it is a wide, car-free, cobbled space with colonial buildings on several sides. It photographs well because the open ground gives you room to step back and fit a whole building into the frame, and the people on the square add life to the picture. The restored former city hall, now the Jakarta History Museum, forms the main backdrop. The square was first recorded around 1627 as the Nieuwe Markt, or New Marketplace. The city hall was made a history museum in 1974, the same year the 18th-century water pump in the middle of the square was restored. The name comes from Fatahillah, a 16th-century commander of the Sultanate of Demak. Other museums, including the Wayang Museum and the Fine Art and Ceramics Museum, are nearby. For a simple, strong picture, put the museum facade behind the open square and let the cobbles lead the eye towards it. Take a second shot with the water pump in the foreground. If you want a view looking down, Cafe Batavia on the square gives a higher angle, but you need to order something to sit at a window. Weekend middays are busy, so expect people in your frame. Costumed performers and bike-renters often expect a small tip if you photograph them.
text.geographic_location: Fatahillah Square is in the middle of Jakarta Old Town (Kota Tua). It is surrounded by the Jakarta History Museum, the Wayang Museum and the Fine Art and Ceramics Museum.
text.directions_text: Check local transport options for getting to the Old Town (Kota Tua) area of Jakarta. The square is car-free, so expect to walk in on foot. The Jakarta History Museum is on that same side. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the long museum facade and the open square into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look and for people in the scene. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it for details such as the windows, the roofline or the water pump.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Museum Sejarah Jakarta (front of the building on the south side of the square). The restored Dutch colonial facade of the former Batavia city hall framed against the open square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the building's vertical edges lined up with them, so the facade does not lean. Include a strip of cobbles in the foreground to give a sense of space. For another angle, try the cobbled square with the water pump in the foreground and the museum behind it, or the elevated view from Cafe Batavia, if you choose to sit there.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the building keeps its colour. Use Live Photos or motion if you want to catch people crossing the square, and then pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, around 8-10 AM, gives soft light. Late afternoon also works. Midday shadows are harsh, and weekend middays are crowded. The best light can vary, so check the conditions on the day.

text.access_note: The square is an open, car-free public space, but the Jakarta History Museum is ticketed and has photography rules (no flash inside), so check the official site before you go.

name: Gelora Bung Karno Stadium
label: Bung Karno Stadium
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/682984153: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Gelora Bung Karno Main Stadium' (419 m across).
notes: The big oval national stadium with its distinctive ring-shaped roof.

text.description: Gelora Bung Karno Stadium, often shortened to GBK, is the main stadium of the Gelora Bung Karno Sports Complex at Senayan, and the 8th largest football stadium in Asia. It opened in 1962, just before that year's Asian Games, and was named after Sukarno, Indonesia's first president. What makes it a good phone subject is the huge ring-shaped roof, which Sukarno pushed for so that it would shade the spectators. It is described as the world's first football stadium with a circular roof, so the shape reads clearly even in a simple, straight-on photo. After the 2018 Asian Games renovation the seats are coloured red, white and grey, like a waving Indonesian flag, and the facade has a colour lighting system. The stadium now holds 77,193 people, down from 110,000 when it opened. Keep your phone level so the ring does not lean, and use the gridlines to help. Zoom in for details of the roof edge and the facade.
text.geographic_location: In the Senayan area of Central Jakarta, at the centre of the Gelora Bung Karno Sports Complex, which also holds the Sports Palace and a secondary stadium.
text.directions_text: No station is listed for this spot. Head for Senayan in Central Jakarta and look for the Gelora Bung Karno Sports Complex. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the full ring of the roof in one frame, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner view with less edge stretching. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the roof edge and facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (in front of the main stadium, facing its façade). The archer statue in the foreground with the stadium's roof and façade behind it, with people jogging or walking on the forecourt.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the phone level, so the ring of the roof looks even rather than tilted. Leave a little space around the stadium so the shape stands out. For a second picture, zoom in with 2x-5x to fill the frame with the roof edge and the lit facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stadium to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the roof does not wash out. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon gives softer light on the roof, and after dusk you may catch the facade lighting. Midday sun is harsher and flattens the shape.

text.access_note: Access around and inside the stadium may vary, so check locally before you go.

name: Merdeka Palace
label: Merdeka Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Medan Merdeka' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Jalan Medan Merdeka Barat' (roads).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1139728: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: The white presidential palace on the north side of Merdeka Square.

text.description:
Merdeka Palace is the white, columned presidential palace on the north side of Merdeka Square in Central Jakarta. It was built as the home of the Dutch governor-general. Work began in 1873 and finished in 1879, to a Neo-Palladian design by Jacobus Bartholomeus Drossaers. It took its present name in 1949, when 'merdeka' (freedom) became the word for the day the Indonesian flag replaced the Dutch one. It is still used for state events, including the Independence Day ceremony on 17 August.

It photographs well because the whole front is clean and symmetrical, and it sits behind open lawn with space around it. A 17 m flagpole and a fountain stand on the front lawn, which gives you a natural centre line and a foreground. The palace is part of a 6.8 ha complex of government buildings, so the view is of one building rather than a busy street scene.

The front of the palace faces south, so the best view is from the southern part of Medan Merdeka, the square in front of it, facing north across the lawn and parade ground at the full facade. Walk on towards the part of the square directly in front of the palace for the straight-on view. A second option is Jalan Medan Merdeka Utara, where you can see the front through the compound gates. This is an active palace, so plan to shoot from outside. Drones are not allowed. Expect barriers and crowds around 17 August.
text.geographic_location: Merdeka Palace is in Central Jakarta, on the north side of Merdeka Square (Medan Merdeka). It is part of the presidential palace complex, next to Istana Negara and the Bina Graha building.
text.directions_text: No station is listed for this spot, so head for Merdeka Square in Central Jakarta by taxi or hired scooter and ask for Medan Merdeka. From there the palace is about 264 m to the east, about 4 minutes on foot. Follow the paths over the open lawn, and for the straight-on view move to the part of the square directly in front of the palace and turn to face north towards the white facade. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the whole facade across the lawn. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the columns, the veranda and the flagpole. Keep the ultra-wide (0.5x) for when you are close, and expect the edges to stretch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Medan Merdeka (southern part of the square, looking north at the palace's south-facing front). The full white neoclassical facade of the palace, with the building framed across the open lawn and parade ground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the palace on the upper line, with lawn in the lower third. Keep the phone level so the columns stay straight. The flagpole or fountain can anchor the foreground, but check they do not cut the building in half. If the square is busy, wait a moment for a gap in the crowd. For a different view, try Jalan Medan Merdeka Utara, where the front can be seen through the gates.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the facade does not turn into a flat white patch against the sky. Skip portrait mode here. Do not fly a drone.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer. Guides disagree a little on which is better, so check the conditions on the day.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but the palace is an active presidential residence with the interior closed except on occasional open days, so shoot from outside and check the official site before you go.

name: Taman Prasasti Museum
label: Taman Prasasti
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jalan Tanah Abang I' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Jalan Tanah Abang I nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/199031142: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Museum Taman Prasasti' (32 m across).
notes: A Dutch-era cemetery turned open-air museum.

text.description:
Taman Prasasti Museum is a former Dutch colonial cemetery in the middle of Jakarta, now run as an open-air museum. Burials began here in 1795 and the cemetery officially opened on 28 September 1797. The grounds were once much larger, but they were cut from 5.9 to 1.3 hectares when the Central Jakarta mayoralty office was built. It became a museum on 9 July 1977. Its graves include Olivia Mariamne Raffles, the first wife of Thomas Stamford Raffles, and the activist Soe Hok Gie. The collection also holds the original coffins of Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta.

It photographs well because the scenes are so varied. Just inside the main gate, a weeping female statue is the first thing visitors meet, and it makes a striking, quiet portrait subject. Further in, old Dutch tombstones stand in rows along the enclosing walls, with trees giving shade. These suit a moody black-and-white shot. Near the entrance, the museum sign and an old cannon sit in front of the building, a popular spot for selfies. The doric-style main building dates from 1874.

On a phone, keep shots simple and move closer to the statues so the details show. Look for stones with interesting carving or weathering, and let the trees frame the edges. If you are shooting people, be respectful, because this is still a burial ground. If you plan anything beyond casual photos, ask the staff first.
text.geographic_location: In Central Jakarta, on Jalan Tanah Abang I, on the former cemetery grounds that were reduced to make way for the Central Jakarta mayoralty office.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so use a map app on your phone to navigate to Jalan Tanah Abang I and the museum's main entrance gate. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the statue and the museum sign. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the cannon and building together, or use telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for carved details on the tombstones.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Jalan Tanah Abang I (main entrance gate, just inside the gate). The weeping female statue that greets visitors as they first enter through the main gate. From here the weeping female statue that greets visitors is your first subject, and the heart of the museum grounds lies a little to the south-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the statue on one of the lines, leaving some space around it. Try a slightly low angle so it stands out against the trees. For a second shot, frame the museum sign and old cannon in the foreground with the building behind them. Or follow the tombstones along the walls and use the rows to lead the eye into the picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the statue to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky behind is bright. For the tombstone rows, try your camera's black-and-white filter or mono mode. Portrait mode can separate the statue from the background if you stand close.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows than midday. Check the opening times before you go.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed museum site and a former burial ground, and fees may apply for commercial or prewedding shoots, so check the official site before you go and ask staff before any professional shoot.

name: Immanuel Church
label: Immanuel Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jalan Medan Merdeka Timur' (4 web pages); placed at crossing of Jalan Medan Merdeka Timur and Jalan Pejambon (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q12483944: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: A domed 19th-century Dutch colonial church beside Gambir station.

text.description: Immanuel Church (Gereja Immanuel, once called Willemskerk) is a Protestant church that photographs well because its shapes are so clear: a pedimented portico with stone columns, and behind it a very broad dark grey-brown dome topped by a small white cupola. It is built of brick in the Indies Empire style and sits on a 3-metre foundation, so the whole building looks raised and calm against the sky. Construction began in 1834, the first stone was laid on 24 August 1835, and it was finished four years later. It was named after King William I of the Netherlands, and it is counted among the oldest churches in Indonesia. The best frontal view, where you can fit the portico, columns and dome into one frame, is from the street corner on Jalan Medan Merdeka Timur, so walk along to that corner rather than shooting from the icon itself. The church is set back behind a large fence, so the view may be partly blocked, and the building has been under refurbishment in the past, so scaffolding is possible. Take one wide shot of the whole front first, then move closer for a tighter shot of the columns or the dome. If you want a different view, Taman Monas offers a distant look at the church across the Gambir station area, though that sightline may have changed.
text.geographic_location: Immanuel Church stands in the Gambir area of central Jakarta, on the corner of Jalan Medan Merdeka Timur and Jalan Pejambon, close to Merdeka Square. This was once part of the 19th-century Weltevreden district.
text.directions_text: Head for the Gambir area beside Merdeka Square and look for the corner of Jalan Medan Merdeka Timur and Jalan Pejambon, where the church stands. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full front. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is narrow and you cannot step back far enough. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the dome and columns.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Jalan Medan Merdeka Timur and Jalan Pejambon (corner facing the church's front facade). The church's front facade with its portico, columns and domed roof, framed from the street corner where the church stands.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and keep the portico centred so the columns stand straight. Hold the phone level to avoid leaning verticals. If the fence gets in the way, move along the corner until you find a clearer gap, or hold the phone close to the bars. Take a second shot with telephoto to pick out the dome and white cupola. Taman Monas gives a distant alternative view of the church.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brick or the columns to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the white details are not washed out against the sky. If you go inside, interior photos are described as allowed without flash, but avoid services.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon is recommended for exterior shots of the church.

text.access_note: The church is a place of worship and services are held there, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and whether the building is open or under refurbishment.
claims_not_in_sources: An ultra-wide lens (0.5x) helps when the pavement is narrow and you cannot step back far enough.
Moving along the street corner or holding the phone close to the fence bars can help avoid the fence in the frame.
Lowering the exposure slider slightly helps keep white architectural details from washing out against a bright sky.

name: West Irian Liberation Monument
label: West Irian Monument
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lapangan Banteng' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/748910286: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Pembebasan Irian Jaya' (36 m across).
notes: A tall statue of a man breaking his chains, in Lapangan Banteng.

text.description: The West Irian Liberation Monument stands in the middle of Lapangan Banteng, a park in Sawah Besar, Central Jakarta. A bare-chested bronze figure with wild hair, arms and legs flung wide, breaks free from his chains. His face is turned to the sky with a shouting expression, and he stands on a tall pedestal in a postwar modernist style. President Sukarno commissioned it after the West New Guinea dispute, and it was officially unveiled on 17 August 1963. The design follows a sketch by the artist Henk Ngantung. The figure itself is about 11 metres tall, and the whole monument is usually given as around 36 metres. Guides vary on the exact height, so treat any single figure as approximate. It photographs well because the sculpture is a strong shape against open sky, with a wide lawn around it for stepping back. The park was once a colonial parade ground, which explains the generous space. Use the lawn for wide shots of family or group photos with the monument rising behind. For a more dramatic picture, crouch low and shoot upwards so the figure fills the sky. Weekend evenings can be busy when the dancing fountain runs, so go early if you want clear frames.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Lapangan Banteng, a public park in Sawah Besar, Central Jakarta. The monument faces west, towards St. Ursula Catholic School across the road from the park.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop at this spot, so head for Lapangan Banteng in Sawah Besar, Central Jakarta, by taxi or hired scooter. The monument stands in the middle of the park, so once you are inside, walk towards the centre and you will see the tall pedestal from a long way off. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole monument and its pedestal in one frame, then switch to the default lens (1x) for group shots. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the bronze figure against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For wide family or group shots, step back onto the open lawn of Lapangan Banteng in front of the monument, where the monument is framed by the green lawn and the park.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: For group photos, place people on the grass and leave the monument rising behind them. Turn on gridlines and keep the pedestal upright against a vertical line so it doesn't lean. For the dramatic version, hold the phone low and tilt it up, using the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the full height, or the telephoto to fill the frame with the figure's outstretched arms.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sky or the figure to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bronze keeps its detail and the sky doesn't wash out. Portrait mode works well for people on the lawn.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon near sunset. Weekend evenings can be crowded when the dancing fountain is running.

text.access_note: The park is an open public space, but the area around the monument's base has been closed off at times (the sides were closed in September 2023), so check current access before you go.

name: Sunda Kelapa
label: Sunda Kelapa
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Menara Syahbandar' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Menara Syahbandar' (way/157513638): middle (14 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1286686: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: The historic port where traditional pinisi schooners dock.

text.description:
Sunda Kelapa is the old port of Jakarta, on the estuary of the Ciliwung River in Penjaringan District, North Jakarta. Today it handles only pinisi, the traditional two-masted wooden sailing ships that carry freight between islands, so you see tall hulls and rigging packed along the quay. Jakarta grew from this harbour. It was the main port of the Sunda Kingdom from the 13th to the 16th century, and the Dutch founded Batavia here in 1619. It is also a working cargo port, which is why it photographs well: wooden schooners, cargo workers and stacked containers share the frame, sometimes with modern apartment blocks behind.

The best overview is from the top floor of Menara Syahbandar, looking across the harbour. From up there you see the moored boats, the canal and the old Kota Tua roofs around them. Guides call it the classic panoramic lookout, and the tilt of the tower is a good subject too when seen from outside. Down at the quay, the pinisi sit close to the water in the foreground. Keep clear of loading gear and workers, and don't ask busy workers for portraits. Late afternoon is a good time to be on the tower. On a phone, shoot a wide view first, then zoom in on a single boat for a second, simpler picture.
text.geographic_location: Sunda Kelapa is in Penjaringan District, North Jakarta, on the Ciliwung River estuary. Menara Syahbandar is about 400 m south of the harbour point, and the Kota Tua roofs can be seen from the top of the tower.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. Navigate to Menara Syahbandar (address most often given as Jl. Pasar Ikan). From the tower, the harbour is about 400 m to the north. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) from the tower to take in the whole harbour and the Kota Tua roofs. Use the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view of the boats. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single pinisi hull and its rigging.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Menara Syahbandar (top floor of the tower, looking across the harbour). An elevated, bird's-eye view of the Sunda Kelapa harbour, moored boats and the canal, with the old Kota Tua roofs around them. The stairs are steep and visitors take turns going up, so be patient and don't linger at the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the line of moored boats along the lower third, with the Kota Tua roofs above. Include a little of the tower's wall or window edge for depth. For a separate shot, photograph the tilted tower itself from the quay or the street outside. For a close-up alternative, go down to the harbour quay (Pelabuhan Sunda Kelapa) and shoot the pinisi in the foreground with workers and containers behind. Keep a safe distance from loading gear.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the boats to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the hulls and rigging keep their detail. Take a Live Photo or a short burst when workers or boats are moving, then pick the best frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, for the sunset light over the harbour.

text.access_note: The harbour is an active cargo port and the tower is a paid entry. The harbour's entry charge, the tower fee and the opening hours can vary, so check on the day.
